title: Genome-wide association study of cocaine self-administration behavior in Heterogeneous Stock rats
abstract: Abstract Background Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is a major public health crisis with detrimental individual and societal effects. The specific genes mediating CUD remain largely unknown. Methods We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) using outbred N/NIH Heterogeneous Stock (HS; n = 836, female = 415, male = 421) rats. We examined multiple CUD-related phenotypes that captured acquisition of self-administration, escalation of intake, and compulsive-like responding. Results Consistent with the existing literature, these traits were phenotypically and genetically correlated and exhibited modest heritability (h 2 = 0.07 – 0.16). We identified six genome-wide significant associations. One locus on chromosome 19 was associated with the variable time between cocaine infusions (post infusion interval) and contains several carboxylesterase genes that are orthologous to the human CES1 gene; notably, carboxylesterases metabolize cocaine. Three non-synonymous coding variants in the genes Ces1c and Ces1d were in perfect linkage disequilibrium with this locus, suggesting that one or more of them might be the causal SNP. The other 5 loci also contained promising coding and expression variants, including Trak2, a gene previously associated with CUD in human GWAS and Slc10a7 , Plcl1 , and Satb2 which have been associated with alcohol and tobacco use disorder. Conclusions This is the largest genetic study of cocaine self-administration ever conducted in any species. Our results replicate previous loci associated with CUD in humans and provide several novel biological insights including the potential of pharmacological strategies targeting carboxylesterases for the treatment of CUD.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2026 Nature Communications article offers an early but credible signal of scholarly uptake in the cocaine-use-disorder literature. It has 2 citations so far, 3 documented reuse events, and signs of methodological attention through two RRID records, which together suggest the work is being taken up as a reproducibility-conscious genetics resource rather than remaining only a standalone report.

Full narrative

The article applies a genome-wide association study to outbred N/NIH Heterogeneous Stock rats to probe the genetic architecture of cocaine self-administration behaviors, including acquisition, escalation, and compulsive-like responding. Its impact record is still early, but the pattern is noteworthy: the paper is already being cited by two 2026 journal articles, one in Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy and one in Psychopharmacology, both in adjacent drug-behavior research areas.

Beyond direct citation, the record shows 3 downstream reuse events, including an article-level reuse and a biomedical article mention in Europe PMC. That combination points to the paper being used as a source of data or methods context in subsequent work, not merely referenced in passing. The citing literature also clusters around drug-response and behavior topics, aligning closely with the study’s focus on cocaine intake patterns in rats.

The stewardship signals are also strong for a 2026 article: the work is linked to an open Zenodo record and carries two RRID entries, indicating attention to resource identification and reproducibility. In a field where animal-model genetics and behavioral phenotyping can be difficult to standardize across studies, that kind of infrastructure matters because it makes the work easier to reuse and validate.

The funding profile—anchored by NIH and NIDA support—fits the article’s translational relevance to substance-use research. Public attention remains limited in the available record, aside from a podcast mention, so the main story is still scholarly and infrastructural rather than broad public reach. Overall, this is an emerging but promising citation and reuse profile for a paper that appears positioned to serve as a reference point for genetics-driven cocaine self-administration research.
